chapter_title: The Chapter of the Four Kingdoms
chapter_note: This kephalaion contains no recoverable correspondential-cosmological substrate. It is a late homiletic unit built around a Gospel saying (bread/cup of water to disciples) and its institutional application (catechumens, alms, reward at the last day), wrapped in a dialogue-style attribution (“the apostle speaks”). The content consistently points from teaching to contemporary religious practice rather than mapping cosmos→cosmos.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic/dialogue attribution marker (“Once again the apostle speaks”) is a compilation-frame feature; not part of the older substrate.

World-historical listing of contemporary ‘great kingdoms’ functions as rhetorical setup for ethical comparison, not as cosmological system-mapping; points to the editor’s present-world geography rather than internal cosmic architecture.

Direct echo/paraphrase of a Gospel saying (gift of bread and water to a disciple ‘on account of the name of God’), cast as an authoritative ‘I say to you in truth’ homily; entered the Kephalaia via NT/Jesus-saying tradition.

Institutional Manichaean application to ‘a catechumen of the truth’ with soteriological reward language (‘rest for ever’). Even though it reuses the Gospel-motif of bread/water, the distinctive addition is church-catechetical practice.

Explicit citation formula (‘Just as the saying that the good saviour uttered’) followed by quotation; by rule, Gospel-derived citation is a later Christian overlay regardless of correspondential content.

Exegetical gloss on the ‘saviour’ calling saints ‘least of the faithful’ plus moral critique of ‘lust of the world’; this is Gospel-based interpretation and exhortational application rather than impersonal cosmological exposition.

Christian-ecclesial theology of indwelling ‘Holy Spirit’ in the faithful/catechumen; this vocabulary and mode (indwelling Spirit + audience address ‘I tell you’) indicates later overlay rather than pre-compilation cosmological correspondences.

Institutional practice language (‘alms’, ‘fellowship with them’) and reward economy (‘thanks before his true father’, ‘repa[y]… at the last day’)—a church disciplinary/hortatory development, not system-description.
Closing exhortation/beatitude-style encouragement (‘Blessed are these who will hear and believe… set their heart…’) is application-voice typical of later paraenesis, not substrate teaching.
